client: I've been really struggling since my dog passed away last month. Things I used to love, like going for walks or watching movies on the couch, just feel hollow now because he was always part of those moments. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should try something because I can't keep feeling this way.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I want you to know that what you're feeling — that hollow ache where joy used to be — makes complete sense after losing such a close companion. Grief has a way of emptying out the things we loved most, at least for a while, because those moments are so tied to who we shared them with. I'm wondering, when you imagine going for a walk now, what kinds of thoughts tend to come up for you in those moments?

client: When I think about going for a walk, the first thing that hits me is that Max used to go with me every single time, and now it just feels like I'd be walking around with this huge absence next to me. I keep thinking people will see me and wonder why I don't have a dog anymore, or maybe I'll run into someone who knew him and have to explain what happened. It sounds silly when I say it out loud, but somehow staying home feels safer than facing all of that.
therapist: It doesn't sound silly at all — it sounds like those walks have become loaded with so many potential painful moments that staying home feels like the only way to protect yourself right now. I'm curious about that thought that people will notice or judge you for not having Max with you — if a close friend were in your situation, would you find yourself thinking that about *them*, or does that standard feel like it applies differently to you? What do you imagine those people are actually thinking when they see someone walking alone?

client: I mean... if a friend told me they lost their dog and couldn't face walking the same route, I wouldn't judge them at all. I'd just feel sad for them. But somehow when it's me, I just assume everyone's looking and thinking "where's her dog, something must be wrong with her" — like I'm walking around with this visible sign of failure or loss. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but the feeling is so strong it's hard to argue with it in the moment.
therapist: You just did something really important there — you noticed that the compassion and understanding you'd freely give a friend somehow doesn't feel available to you when you're the one hurting, and that gap is so worth paying attention to. That thought of being a "visible sign of failure" is a really painful lens to see yourself through, and it makes sense that it feels hard to argue with in the moment even when part of you can see it isn't quite fair. I'm wondering — what do you think it would feel like to try offering yourself even just a little of that same gentleness you'd give your friend, maybe just as an experiment on a short walk?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, part of me wants to try it, but another part just feels kind of silly about it, like I'd be pretending or lying to myself. Because when I'm actually out there walking alone, that voice that says I'm a failure doesn't feel like a distortion — it feels like the truth, and I don't know how to argue with something that feels so real. I guess I'm worried that trying to be gentle with myself will just feel hollow, like putting a bandage on something that actually needs stitches.
therapist: That tension you're describing — between wanting to try and fearing it will feel fake — is actually really common, and it doesn't mean self-compassion won't work for you, it just means grief has made that inner critic's voice feel very loud and authoritative right now. The goal isn't to pretend the pain isn't there or to convince yourself everything is fine — it's actually closer to what a good doctor does, acknowledging the wound is real *and* still tending to it carefully. I'm curious, when you imagine what "tending to yourself" might look like on that walk — not fixing the grief, just accompanying yourself through it — what would that actually look like for you?

client: I guess... maybe it would look like not rushing. Like, not having my headphones in trying to drown everything out, which is what I usually do. But even as I say that, I feel this pull to fill the silence because when it's quiet, that's when I really feel how alone I am in all of this.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what you just described — that image of slowing down, not armoring yourself with noise, even though the quiet is where the grief lives most honestly. It sounds like part of you already knows what gentleness might look like, even if it feels scary to actually let yourself be present with that silence. I'm wondering, when you say you feel alone in all of this — do you mean alone on the walks, or does that feeling of aloneness stretch further than that?

client: It stretches a lot further than the walks, honestly. It's more like... even when I'm around people, there's this feeling that nobody really gets what's going on inside me, like I'm speaking a language nobody else knows. And then I feel guilty for even thinking that, because I have people in my life who care, so who am I to say I'm alone?
therapist: That feeling of being surrounded by care and yet still feeling fundamentally unseen is one of the loneliest experiences there is, and the guilt you're adding on top of it — telling yourself you don't have the right to feel that way — is like a second layer of pain on top of the first. Grief over a pet is often quietly minimized by the world around us, which can make it really hard to feel like others can truly meet you where you are, even when they love you. I'm curious — is there anyone in your life who you feel has come even close to understanding what losing Max has meant to you, or has it mostly felt like you've been carrying this privately?

client: There's one person, maybe — my friend Carla reached out a few days after and said she'd lost a dog years ago and still thought about him sometimes. That helped a little, but even then it felt like we were talking about her experience more than mine, and I didn't want to seem like I was competing over who had it worse. Mostly it's just been me, going home to an empty apartment and trying not to look at his water bowl that I still haven't moved.
therapist: That image of his water bowl still sitting there says so much — it's like moving it would make the loss more final, and yet seeing it every day keeps the ache right at the surface, and there's no easy way through that. It's also really tender that even with Carla, you were protecting her feelings and managing the conversation rather than letting yourself be the one who needed something for once. I'm wondering — what do you think would happen if you let yourself need a little more space in a conversation, like with Carla, rather than quietly stepping aside?

client: I think if I let myself take up more space, I'd just end up making Carla uncomfortable or she'd feel like she said the wrong thing and then I'd feel guilty about that. It's almost easier to just... manage it quietly so no one has to feel awkward. I know that probably sounds like I'm making excuses, but I genuinely don't know how to let someone help me without it turning into me taking care of them anyway.
therapist: What you're describing isn't an excuse at all — it sounds like you've become so practiced at keeping others comfortable that it's genuinely hard to imagine a version of being helped that doesn't somehow loop back to you doing the emotional work. That pattern makes a lot of sense as a way of staying safe, but it also means you've been carrying this grief almost entirely alone, which is an exhausting way to live. I'm curious — where do you think you learned that taking up space or needing something from others was something that had to be carefully managed or earned?

client: I think I learned it pretty early, honestly — my mom was dealing with a lot when I was growing up, and I just kind of figured out that adding my stuff to her pile wasn't going to help anyone. It became this automatic thing, like I'd scan the room before deciding if I was allowed to feel something. I guess I never really stopped doing that, even now that she's gone and I'm the one who's grieving her.
therapist: What you just shared is profound — that little version of you learned to scan for permission before feeling anything, and that was such a wise and loving adaptation for a child trying not to add to her mother's burden. But you're carrying two griefs right now, Max and your mom, and that same old pattern is still quietly telling you that your pain needs to wait for a room that's ready for it. I'm wondering — what do you think that younger version of you would feel, knowing that you're still waiting for permission to grieve, even now?

client: I think she'd feel... sad, maybe. Like, she did all that work to hold herself together, and here I am still doing the same thing decades later. But honestly, Luna, part of me is also a little resistant to this framing, because it almost makes my grief sound like a pattern to fix rather than just... something real that's happening to me right now.
therapist: That resistance is really important and I'm glad you named it, because you're absolutely right — your grief is not a pattern to be fixed, it's a real and valid response to real losses, and I never want this to feel like we're pathologizing your pain or turning it into a problem to solve. What I'm more interested in is making sure the grief actually gets to breathe and be felt, rather than being quietly managed away like you've had to do with so many feelings before. So I want to ask — what would it mean to you to just let this grief be real and present, without needing to understand it or fix it or protect anyone from it, even just for a moment?
